items.topic: What the licence is for, and where it applies

F.note: The amateur licence is for self-training in radio and is strictly non-commercial: no business use, no advertising. It covers the UK, the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man (including their territorial seas), and UK-registered ships and aircraft in international waters or airspace. It does not let you transmit in other countries.

q.text: Which of these is allowed under a UK amateur licence?
choices: Advertising a radio for sale for your business
Operating from a hotel balcony in France on your UK licence alone
q.why: The licence is for non-commercial self-training. Business use is banned, and it doesn't cover other countries.

items.topic: Licence types, call signs, RSLs and suffixes

F.note: There are three personal licences: Foundation, Intermediate and Full. A Regional Secondary Locator (RSL) shows where you are: D Isle of Man, E England, I Northern Ireland, J Jersey, M Scotland, U Guernsey, W Wales. RSLs are now optional, except in the older 2-series Intermediate calls (2E0, 2M0…), where they're required. If you use one it must be the right one. You may add a suffix such as /P or /M, as long as it isn't offensive and doesn't stop you being identified. Foundation licensees have restrictions when operating from ships or aircraft.

q.text: A Foundation licensee operating in Scotland chooses to use a Regional Secondary Locator. Which letter must it be?
q.why: M is Scotland (as in GM, MM). W is Wales, E England.

q.text: Which statement about suffixes such as /P is correct?
choices: Any suffix is allowed if it isn't offensive and you can still be identified
A suffix replaces the need to give your call sign
q.why: Since 2024 any suffix may be used, provided it doesn't obscure identification or cause offence.

I.note: Intermediate licensees also have particular restrictions when operating from a ship or aircraft, and these differ from the Full licence. Airborne operation is limited to low power in the bands where amateurs are primary users.

q.text: Airborne amateur operation under the UK licence is limited to…
choices: Low power, in bands where amateurs have a primary allocation
q.why: Airborne use is allowed only at low power (500 mW EIRP) and only in primary allocations.

F.note: Tell Ofcom straight away if your name or address changes. You must confirm your licence details are still correct at least once every five years. Ofcom can revoke a licence for breaking its conditions.

q.text: How often must you confirm (revalidate) your licence details with Ofcom?
choices: At least once every five years
Never: the licence is for life without checks
q.why: The licence lasts for life, but the details must be confirmed at least every five years.

F.note: Give your call sign clearly so others know who's transmitting: at the start and end of each period of transmission, and regularly during it. Identify again whenever you change frequency, mode (CW, SSB, FM, AM or data such as FT8), supervisor, or the RSL you're using.

q.text: You switch from CW to SSB on the same frequency. What must you do?
choices: Identify again with your call sign
Nothing, since the frequency hasn't changed
q.why: A change of mode is one of the occasions when you must identify.

F.note: Only the licensee, or someone under the licensee's direct supervision, may use the Radio Equipment. An unlicensed guest can operate under supervision. The station then uses the supervisor's call sign and works to the supervisor's licence conditions. A visiting amateur who uses their own call sign is treated as using their own Radio Equipment.

q.text: Your unlicensed friend wants to try a contact under your direct supervision. Which call sign is used?
choices: Theirs, once they've passed the exam
q.why: Supervised operation identifies with the supervisor's call sign and follows the supervisor's licence.

I.note: Direct supervision means being present and in control: you must be able to stop the transmission immediately, and you're responsible for everything sent. The operator must still follow the licence conditions.

q.text: Who is responsible for what's transmitted when a guest operates under supervision?
q.why: The licensee remains responsible for all transmissions under their licence.

F.note: Send messages only to other amateur stations, and only on UK amateur frequencies. A net is a group of three or more amateurs in contact. You mustn't broadcast to 'anyone listening', except when calling CQ.

q.text: Which transmission is allowed?
choices: Calling CQ to look for a contact
Sending messages to a CB user
q.why: General broadcasting isn't allowed; a CQ call is the exception.

I.note: During an international disaster, amateurs may pass messages internationally on behalf of people who aren't licensed. Non-amateur stations involved in disaster communications may also be heard on amateur frequencies then.

q.text: When may you pass a message internationally on behalf of an unlicensed person?
q.why: Third-party traffic internationally is permitted in international disaster situations.

Full.note: Content matters. People of every age and background listen, so messages must never cause offence (the Wireless Telegraphy (Content of Transmission) Regulations 1988 and the Communications Act 2003 apply). Codes and abbreviations such as Q-codes are fine because their meaning is public. Encryption, which hides meaning, is only allowed at the request of a User Service.

q.text: Why are Q-codes allowed when encryption generally isn't?
choices: Their meanings are published, so they don't hide the message
Ofcom issues a special permit for them
q.why: Abbreviations whose meaning is public aren't secret codes; encryption obscures meaning.

F.note: Encryption isn't permitted except at the direct request of a User Service (such as an emergency service). Morse code is not a secret code: only codes meant to hide a message's meaning are banned.

q.text: Is sending in Morse code a breach of the ban on encryption?
choices: No: Morse isn't a secret code
q.why: Morse is a public code; only secret codes that obscure meaning are prohibited.

I.note: You may pass messages on behalf of a User Service and may let its members use your Radio Equipment to send them.

q.text: A User Service asks you to relay messages for them. Is this allowed?
choices: Yes, you may pass messages for a User Service
Only if they hold a Full licence
q.why: The licence allows messages on behalf of User Services, and lets them use your equipment.

F.note: You must not cause Undue Interference to other radio users. A person authorised by Ofcom can inspect your station, require changes, restrict your operation or require it to close down.

q.text: A person authorised by Ofcom visits about interference you're causing. What can they require?
choices: Inspection, modification, restriction or closedown of your station
Payment of a fine on the spot
q.why: Authorised persons have the right to inspect, require modification, restrict or close down the equipment.

I.note: If your station causes interference, you must reduce the offending emissions to the satisfaction of a person authorised by Ofcom, for example by cutting power or fixing the cause.

q.text: Your transmissions interfere with a neighbour's TV and Ofcom gets involved. What may you be asked to do?
choices: Reduce the emissions, for example by cutting power, to Ofcom's satisfaction
q.why: The licensee must reduce interfering emissions to the satisfaction of a person authorised by Ofcom.

Full.note: Keep transmitters clean and stable, and control your transmitted bandwidth. Check from time to time that you're not causing interference. Be able to receive on every frequency and mode you transmit on. Ofcom investigates and enforces in cases of Undue Interference.

q.text: Why must you be able to receive on every frequency and mode you transmit on?
choices: So you can hear if the channel's busy and respond to other stations
q.why: Being able to listen prevents interference and lets you hear calls to you.

items.topic: Logs and changes to your station

F.note: A person authorised by Ofcom can require you to keep a log of all your transmissions for a set period.

q.text: When might you be required to keep a log of all transmissions?
choices: When a person authorised by Ofcom requires it for a set period
q.why: Ofcom can require a log over a specified period.

I.note: Know when keeping a log is compulsory, and that Ofcom may require you to modify equipment or stop operating, for example if it causes interference or doesn't meet the licence conditions.

q.text: Which could lead to you being required to stop operating until equipment is modified?
choices: Your transmitter producing spurious emissions that interfere with others
q.why: Interference or non-compliance can lead to required modification or cessation.

I.note: You may control your station remotely over any communication link, including the internet, but the link must be secure so nobody else can take control. You must be able to stop transmissions promptly. Remote-control links on amateur frequencies must be above 30 MHz and not encrypted. If unattended equipment is away from your licensed address, the licence number must be shown on or next to it.

q.text: You control your station by a radio link on an amateur band. Which rule applies to that link?
choices: It must be above 30 MHz and not encrypted
It must be encrypted for security
q.why: Amateur-band remote control links must be above 30 MHz and unencrypted.

Full.note: Any communication link may be used for remote control. A link on an amateur band must meet the same licence rules as the main station, be above 30 MHz, and not be encrypted.

q.text: A remote-control link on 70 cm must…
choices: Meet the same licence requirements as the main station, unencrypted
Use a different call sign from the station
q.why: An amateur-band link carries the same licence requirements as the main station and mustn't be encrypted.

F.note: Other countries don't routinely recognise the Foundation licence, so you can't simply take it abroad.

q.text: Can a Foundation licensee operate on holiday in Spain using their UK licence?
choices: Not routinely: Foundation isn't generally recognised abroad
q.why: Foundation (and Intermediate) licences aren't routinely recognised by other administrations.

I.note: The Intermediate licence isn't routinely recognised by other countries either.

q.text: Is the Intermediate licence routinely recognised in other countries?
q.why: Only the Full licence gives access to CEPT arrangements.

Full.note: Under the CEPT T/R 61-01 arrangement, Full licensees can operate temporarily in participating countries, following the host country's rules; this doesn't cover club or reciprocal licences. The HAREC certificate shows you've passed an exam at the harmonised CEPT standard, and many countries will issue a reciprocal licence on that basis.

q.text: What is HAREC?
choices: A certificate showing an exam passed to the harmonised CEPT standard
q.why: HAREC is the Harmonised Amateur Radio Examination Certificate.

Full.note: The ITU divides the world into three regions for frequency allocation: Region 1 (Europe, Africa, the Middle East and northern Asia, including the UK), Region 2 (the Americas) and Region 3 (most of Asia and Oceania). The allocations are set out in the ITU Radio Regulations.

q.text: Which ITU region is the UK in?
q.why: Region 1 covers Europe, Africa, the Middle East and northern Asia.

F.note: Strong radio-frequency fields can harm people, so the licence sets basic EMF restrictions (based on ICNIRP guidelines) to protect the general public. Above the power threshold in the licence you must assess your station, and keep a record of the assessment, including the reasoning when no further action is needed.

q.text: What must you keep after carrying out an EMF assessment?
choices: A record of it, including why any further action isn't needed
q.why: A record of each assessment must be kept, with justification.

I.note: Know the power level at which the EMF rules apply, both average and peak, and when you must reassess: for example, after changing antenna, power or location.

q.text: When should you redo your EMF assessment?
choices: After a significant change, such as a new antenna or more power
q.why: Material changes to the station mean the assessment must be reviewed.

Full.note: The limits come from ICNIRP. The 'general public' means people who aren't aware of, or able to control, their exposure. Know where they need protecting, how to carry out and record an assessment, and that there are special provisions for emergencies.

q.text: Where do the EMF exposure limits in the licence come from?
q.why: The basic restrictions are based on ICNIRP guidance.

F.note: Schedule 1 of the licence lists the bands, power limits and status you may use. Primary status means amateurs have priority; secondary means you must not interfere with primary users and must accept interference from them. A copy is provided in the exam. The 2024 limits are 25 W for Foundation, 100 W for Intermediate, and up to 1 kW for Full in primary bands. Foundation also has 2.4 and 5 GHz at 2 W.

q.text: In a band where amateurs have secondary status, you must…
choices: Not interfere with primary users and accept interference from them
Have priority over all other users
q.why: Secondary users mustn't cause interference to, and can't claim protection from, primary users.

q.text: What is the maximum power for a Foundation licensee in most HF bands since 2024?
q.why: Foundation went up to 25 W; Intermediate is 100 W; Full up to 1 kW in primary bands.

I.note: At Intermediate, use Schedule 1 to work out what's allowed in a given band: frequencies, power, modes and status.

q.text: What is the Intermediate power limit in bands where the Full licence permits 400 W?
q.why: Intermediate is 100 W PEP since 2024.

Full.note: At Full, read Schedule 1 together with the Notice of coordination; both are provided in the exam.

q.text: Where does a Full licensee look up the bands, powers and status they may use?
q.why: Schedule 1 sets out frequencies, powers and status.
